steps: Acute: NSAID (e.g. naproxen) or paracetamol; add an oral triptan (e.g. sumatriptan 50–100 mg) if no vascular contraindication.
Add an antiemetic (metoclopramide / prochlorperazine) for nausea.
Treat early; rest in a dark, quiet room.
Limit acute drugs to <10–15 days/month to avoid medication-overuse headache.
Prophylaxis if frequent/disabling: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate or candesartan.

drugRefs.freq: at onset, may repeat once after 6–8 h (max 1000 mg/day)
drugRefs.why: Effective acute treatment; take early in the attack.

drugRefs.freq: up to four times daily (max 4 g/day)
drugRefs.why: Alternative simple analgesic for milder attacks or where NSAIDs are contraindicated.

drugRefs.freq: at onset; may repeat after 2 h if response then recurrence (max 300 mg/day)
drugRefs.why: Migraine-specific abortive. Avoid in ischaemic heart/cerebrovascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.
Relieves nausea and improves absorption of oral analgesics. Prochlorperazine is an alternative.

drugRefs.dose: 10 mg at night, titrate to 25–75 mg
drugRefs.why: Useful preventive, especially with coexisting sleep disturbance or tension-type headache.
Effective preventive. Teratogenic and reduces hormonal contraceptive efficacy — counsel women of childbearing potential.
Preventive option, particularly where beta-blockers are unsuitable.

confirm: Recurrent moderate–severe, often unilateral throbbing headache ± aura, photophobia, nausea with a normal exam (ICHD-3). Image only for red flags.
disposition: Outpatient; neurology referral if refractory or atypical.
